doc.title: Pete Barbutti interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 8, 2022

title: Bombing: Plimpton, bad audiences and Steel Pier
summary: Rowe's ten-minute comedy attempt, George Plimpton's eight minutes at Caesars, and bad audiences like Smokey Robinson's.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah. They’ve all experienced it in some fashion. Yeah. As time went by did you find that filling a half an hour or whatever got easier? I shouldn’t talk about myself but I want to tell you that I was in a rock band for a while and somehow I ended up doing a 10- minute opening comedy routine. And I called myself Billy Schechter. And I found it was the hardest thing I’ve ever done.
Only ten minutes, and I would put cue cards on the floor to look down if I couldn’t think of what to talk about.

Well I’m going to tell you a perfect analogy of that. For some reason I’ve done a couple of shows with George Plimpton, the author. And you know George Plimpton, before he writes he does it. He played football with the Chicago Bears and he got busted up bad. Then he did a trapeze thing and threw his back out, but he does everything before he writes it. And George came to Vegas to do a comedy routine at Ceasar’s Palace, and he worked with Milton Berle and Alan King and Cosby. They said to him, “Do this: Light a cigarette when you do this, put your hand in your pocket,” they told him what to do. And one night at Ceasar’s Palace, I forget who was headlining, but they announced a special treat today we have a new comic, and they didn’t use his right name. And so George Plimpton went out on stage and he did like eight minutes. And George Plimpton, we were talking about it on Merv’s show. And George Plimpton said, “Merv,” he says, “of all the things I’ve ever done, you know and I threw my back out and how incredibly painful that

is and when I broke my collar bone” he said, “none of those things came close to the pain that I suffered those eight minutes on stage with the entire audience looking at me and they hated me.” He said, “It’s a — it really is the worst death I’ve ever suffered in my life.”
Did you ever suffer the death like that?

Yeah sometimes it happens. You know Al Jolson was nuts when he said no such thing as a bad audience. You get audiences — somebody did a test many, many years ago, maybe 75 years ago or something, in New York City where they had every entity that had entertainment call in to a certain phone bank and rate the audiences after each show. And they kept records. And the funny part was except for a real rare exception the funny part was when the show at the Copacabana, the audience was bad, the audience was bad at the Latin Quarter. There’s some atmospheric, who knows, vibes, news, something in the news that day that changes your perspective. But yeah, you get a bad audience. But it’s happened to all of us. Even Shecky talks about it, you know, and he was the King of the Kings. He said, “I really bombed here, bombed there, you know, so you learn. And sometimes you’re in a bad situation — you know they booked me at the Steel Pier in Atlantic City opening for Smokey Robinson and the Miracles. Well you know that audience, they were all kids who wanted to see Smokey Robinson. They were yelling and screaming. And you can’t do my act.
Yeah. So what does that mean. So it’s just a bad booking.
